title: A Problem in Your Community
prompt:
Write an essay about a problem in your community and how we might solve it. “Community” might refer to your neighborhood, school, grade, city, state, country, age group, race, gender, or any other group you belong to. Your essay can focus on any problems that you see or feel.

Use your personal experience and observations to develop your position, and evidence from your own experience to support your ideas. How do you propose we solve this problem?

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: A Problem in Education
prompt:
Write a critical essay that discusses a problem in education. It might be something you’ve noticed in your own school, in your own classes, or in the way school works more broadly — how students are tested, what gets taught, who gets heard, or anything else you feel strongly about.

Use your personal experience and observations to develop your position, and evidence from your own experience to support your ideas. How do you propose we solve this problem?

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: What Gives You Hope
prompt:
Write an essay about what gives you hope in the world today. When you look around at the world and all of its complexity, and you look ahead to the future, what gives you hope? You might identify problems that you believe you and your generation can solve, changes or innovations that you look forward to, or people and things that inspire your hope in the face of adversity.

Your essay can include how you define hope, what hope looks like for you personally, or the role hope plays in shaping the state of the world today. You might consider the quote, “If despair creates problems, hope can achieve the impossible.” You may use your personal experiences and observations to develop your stance, and evidence from your own life to support your ideas. In some cases, you may use outside sources to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: A Belief You’ve Changed Your Mind About
prompt:
Write an essay about a belief you once held that you no longer hold. What did you used to think — about yourself, about other people, or about the way the world works — and what changed your mind?

Consider what experience, conversation, or piece of evidence made you reconsider, and what it cost you or freed you to let the old belief go. If you’re having trouble choosing, go where the emotional charge is: pick the belief whose change still feels significant to you. Use your personal experience and observations to develop your position, and evidence from your own life to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: A Rule Worth Questioning
prompt:
Write an essay that makes the case for changing a rule, norm, or expectation you think is wrong. It might be a rule at your school, an unwritten expectation in your community, or a norm most people take for granted.

Be specific about what the rule is, who it affects, and why the usual justification for it doesn’t hold up. Then argue for what should replace it. Use your personal experience and observations to develop your position, and evidence from your own experience to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: What We Owe One Another
prompt:
Write an essay about what we owe one another. What responsibilities, if any, do people have to their families, their neighbors, strangers, or future generations — and where do those responsibilities end?

You might ground your argument in a moment when someone showed up for you, or a moment when you had to decide whether to show up for someone else. Use your personal experience and observations to develop your position, and evidence from your own life to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: Ambition and Its Costs
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven essay about ambition and what it costs. Drawing on a text we’ve read together, explore what the story suggests about the drive to rise, to win, or to become something more — and what a character gives up in the pursuit.

You might focus on a single character whose ambition drives the story, or compare two characters who want the same thing for different reasons. Consider whether the text treats ambition as a virtue, a danger, or both. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the text to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: Justice and Loyalty in Conflict
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven essay about what happens when justice and loyalty pull in opposite directions. Using a text we’ve read, examine a moment when a character has to choose between doing what’s right and standing by someone they love.

Consider what the text seems to value more, and whether you agree. You might argue that the character chose well, or that the story itself is making a case for one loyalty over another. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the text to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: Growing Up and the Loss of Innocence
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven essay about growing up. Using a text we’ve read, explore how a character changes as they lose some illusion about the world, other people, or themselves — and what they gain or lose in the process.

You might trace a single turning point, or follow a character across the whole story. Consider whether the text treats growing up as a gift, a wound, or something more complicated. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the text to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: Power and the People Who Hold It
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven essay about power. Using a text we’ve read, examine how power is won, used, or lost — and what it reveals about the people who hold it.

You might focus on a character who gains power and is changed by it, on the people that power is used against, or on the way the text itself seems to define power. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the text to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: Romeo and Juliet
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven critical essay on Romeo and Juliet. You can choose any aspect of the play that interests you. Consider the themes we’ve discussed, the characters, the settings, or anything you’ve noticed about the story that you think is worthy of discussion.

In figuring out what to write about, consider your favorite character or favorite scene. What about this play entertained you or upset you? Maybe you liked the language of the play and how that affected your experience as a reader. Maybe a particular theme resonated with you. Maybe there’s a specific, favorite character you want to discuss. If you go to your emotional charge — what you loved, what grabbed your attention — you’ll find your topic.

Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the play to support your ideas. Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: Macbeth
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven critical essay on Macbeth. You can choose any aspect of the play that interests you — the themes we’ve discussed, the characters, the imagery, or anything about the story you think is worth discussing.

Maybe you’re drawn to how ambition unravels Macbeth, to the role Lady Macbeth plays, or to the way guilt haunts the language of the play. Start with the scene or character that grabbed you and build your argument from there. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the play to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: The Great Gatsby
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven critical essay on The Great Gatsby. You can choose any aspect of the novel that interests you — the themes we’ve discussed, the characters, the setting, or the way Fitzgerald tells the story.

Maybe you want to argue about who is really responsible for the novel’s tragedy, about what the green light or the valley of ashes means, or about whether Gatsby is admirable or deluded. Begin with what fascinated or bothered you, and let that lead you to your thesis. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the novel to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: To Kill a Mockingbird
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven critical essay on To Kill a Mockingbird. You can choose any aspect of the novel that interests you — the themes we’ve discussed, the characters, the narrator, or anything about the story you think is worth discussing.

Maybe you want to write about what Scout learns and how, about Atticus as a father or as a lawyer, or about how the town itself functions as a character. Start with the moment in the book that stayed with you and build your argument from there. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the novel to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: Of Mice and Men
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven critical essay on Of Mice and Men. You can choose any aspect of the novella that interests you — the themes we’ve discussed, the characters, the setting, or the choices Steinbeck makes as a storyteller.

Maybe you want to argue about George’s final decision, about what the dream of the farm really represents, or about how loneliness shapes every character on the ranch. Begin with what moved or unsettled you, and let that guide your thesis. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the novella to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: A Critical Essay on the Book We Just Read
prompt:
Write a critical essay about the book we just read for class. You can choose any aspect of the book that interests you. Consider the themes we’ve discussed, the characters, the settings, or anything you’ve noticed about the story that you think is worthy of discussion.

Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the book to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: A Character Who Stayed With You
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven essay about a character from a text we’ve read who stayed with you. Choose someone you found yourself thinking about after you closed the book — someone you admired, distrusted, pitied, or couldn’t quite figure out.

Make an argument about who this character really is, what drives them, or how they change. Don’t just describe them; take a position other readers might disagree with. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the text to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: The Moment Everything Turns
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven essay about the turning point in a text we’ve read. Identify the single moment where the story — or a character — changes course, and argue for why that moment matters more than any other.

Consider what is different before and after, and what the author does to make the moment land. You might even argue that the real turning point isn’t the obvious one. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the text to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: Argue With the Author
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven essay that argues with the author of a text we’ve read. Identify a claim the text seems to make — about people, society, right and wrong, or the way the world works — and take a position on whether the author gets it right.

You might agree and push the idea further, disagree and explain where the text goes wrong, or complicate the claim by showing where it holds and where it breaks down. Be fair to the text before you challenge it. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the text to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: What History Means to You
prompt:
Using a specific historical figure, era, movement, or event, write an essay about what history means to you. Use your existing knowledge of history, as well as your personal experience and observations, to develop your position.

You might consider how the specific person, event, or movement aligns with your beliefs or worldview, or how they have shaped your opinions. You might also consider what they teach you about the world, our country, or people in general. If you’re having trouble choosing, go where the emotional charge is: start with what you find interesting, fascinating, or upsetting; choose a historical figure that you really admire or despise.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, supporting evidence, and a conclusion.

title: A Turning Point in History
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven essay about a turning point in history — a moment, decision, or event that you believe changed the course of things. Choose something you actually find compelling, from any period or place.

Make an argument about why this turning point mattered: what the world was like before, what changed, and what might have happened otherwise. Use your existing knowledge of history, along with your own observations, to develop your position, and evidence to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, supporting evidence, and a conclusion.

title: An Idea from Science That Changed the World
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven essay about a scientific idea, discovery, or invention that changed the world. Choose something that genuinely interests you — a theory, a technology, or a breakthrough whose effects you can still see today.

Make an argument about why it mattered: what people believed or could do before, what the idea made possible, and what it cost or complicated along the way. Use your existing knowledge and your own observations to develop your position, and evidence to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, supporting evidence, and a conclusion.

title: A Work of Art That Moves You
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven essay about a work of art that moves you — a painting, a song, an album, a film, a building, or any created thing. Choose one you have a real reaction to, and make an argument about why it works and what it does to the people who encounter it.

Go beyond saying you like it: analyze the choices the artist made and connect them to the effect the work has. You might argue about what the work means, why it lasts, or why it matters now. Use your observations to develop your position, and specific details from the work to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: Fate and Free Will
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven essay about fate and free will. Using a text we’ve read, argue about how much control the characters really have over what happens to them — and how much is decided by forces beyond them.

You might focus on a character who fights their fate, one who accepts it, or the way the text itself seems to answer the question. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the text to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: Belonging and the Outsider
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven essay about belonging. Using a text we’ve read, explore what it means to be an insider or an outsider in the world of the story — who belongs, who doesn’t, and what the difference costs.

You might follow a character who is kept out, one who is let in, or the group that decides. Consider what the text is saying about the price of fitting in. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the text to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: Love and Sacrifice
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven essay about love and what it asks people to give up. Using a text we’ve read, examine a relationship in the story and argue about what love demands of the characters — and whether it’s worth the cost.

You might focus on romantic love, family love, or loyalty between friends. Consider whether the text treats sacrifice as noble, foolish, or something in between. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the text to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: The Individual vs. Society
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven essay about the individual against society. Using a text we’ve read, examine a character who stands apart from the rules, values, or expectations of the world around them, and argue about what the conflict reveals.

You might consider whether the character is right to resist, what it costs them, or what the text is saying about the society itself. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the text to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: Appearance vs. Reality
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven essay about the gap between appearance and reality. Using a text we’ve read, examine where things — a character, a relationship, a whole world — are not what they seem, and argue about what the text is doing with that gap.

You might focus on a character who wears a mask, a truth that stays hidden, or the moment the illusion breaks. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the text to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: Guilt and Conscience
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven essay about guilt. Using a text we’ve read, examine how a character lives with something they’ve done — or failed to do — and argue about what the story is saying about conscience.

You might trace how guilt changes a character, how they try to escape or answer for it, or what the text suggests about whether they can. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the text to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: The Odyssey
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven critical essay on The Odyssey. You can choose any aspect of the poem that interests you — the themes we’ve discussed, the characters, the gods, or anything about the story you think is worth discussing.

Maybe you want to argue about what makes Odysseus a hero — or whether he is one — about the role of hospitality or temptation, or about what home means in the poem. Start with the episode that grabbed you and build your argument from there. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the poem to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: Lord of the Flies
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven critical essay on Lord of the Flies. You can choose any aspect of the novel that interests you — the themes we’ve discussed, the characters, the island, or the choices Golding makes as a storyteller.

Maybe you want to argue about what the novel says about human nature, about what the conch or the beast represents, or about which boy is most responsible for what happens. Begin with what unsettled or fascinated you, and let that lead you to your thesis. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the novel to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: The Catcher in the Rye
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven critical essay on The Catcher in the Rye. You can choose any aspect of the novel that interests you — the themes we’ve discussed, Holden as a narrator, the world he moves through, or anything you noticed.

Maybe you want to argue about whether Holden is a reliable narrator, about what he’s really running from, or about what the novel is saying about growing up. Start with the moment that stayed with you and build from there. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the novel to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: Fahrenheit 451
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven critical essay on Fahrenheit 451. You can choose any aspect of the novel that interests you — the themes we’ve discussed, the characters, the world Bradbury builds, or the choices he makes as a storyteller.

Maybe you want to argue about what the novel warns us against, about what fire means across the book, or about whether its vision of the future has come true. Begin with what fascinated or worried you, and let that lead you to your thesis. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the novel to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: Night
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven critical essay on Night by Elie Wiesel. You can choose any aspect of the memoir that interests you — the themes we’ve discussed, the relationships, the questions it raises, or the choices Wiesel makes in telling his story.

Because of the subject, approach it with care and specificity: you might write about faith and its loss, about the bond between father and son, or about what it means to bear witness. Use your observations and quotations from the text to develop and support your position.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: Their Eyes Were Watching God
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven critical essay on Their Eyes Were Watching God. You can choose any aspect of the novel that interests you — the themes we’ve discussed, Janie’s journey, the language and voice, or anything you noticed.

Maybe you want to argue about what Janie is searching for, about what the horizon or the pear tree represents, or about how each of her relationships changes her. Start with what moved you and build your argument from there. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the novel to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: A Raisin in the Sun
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven critical essay on A Raisin in the Sun. You can choose any aspect of the play that interests you — the themes we’ve discussed, the members of the Younger family, the dreams that drive them, or the choices Hansberry makes as a playwright.

Maybe you want to argue about whose dream matters most, about what the money really represents, or about what the play is saying about family and dignity. Begin with the character or scene that grabbed you. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the play to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: The Villain’s Point of View
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven essay that reconsiders the antagonist of a text we’ve read. Take the character most readers are meant to root against, and argue for a more complicated view of who they are and what drives them.

Be fair to the text: use what’s actually on the page to show where the character’s motives are more understandable — or more disturbing — than they first appear. Don’t excuse them; explain them. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the text to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: A Symbol Worth Unpacking
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven essay about a symbol in a text we’ve read. Choose an object, image, or place that the author returns to, and argue for what it means and how it deepens the story.

Trace where the symbol appears and how its meaning shifts. Make a claim other readers might push back on, rather than simply cataloguing every mention. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the text to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: The Title’s Meaning
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven essay about the title of a text we’ve read. Argue for what the title really means and why the author chose it — what it reveals, hides, or promises about the story.

Consider how your understanding of the title changes from the first page to the last. Use the title as a lens to make a larger claim about the text. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the text to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: An Ending You’d Rewrite
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven essay about the ending of a text we’ve read. Argue about whether the ending is the right one — whether it earns its final note, cheats the reader, or is more fitting than it first seems.

You might defend the ending, argue for how it should have gone, or show what the author gains by ending exactly here. Ground every claim in the text. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the text to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: The Setting as a Character
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven essay about the setting of a text we’ve read. Argue that the time and place aren’t just a backdrop — that they shape the characters and the story as powerfully as any person in it.

Show how the setting presses on the characters’ choices, moods, or fates. Make a claim about what the story would lose somewhere else. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the text to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: A Speech That Changed Minds
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven essay about a speech that changed minds. Choose a speech from any time or place that you find powerful, and argue about how it works and why it mattered.

Look closely at what the speaker says and how they say it — the words, the timing, the audience. Then make a claim about the effect the speech had or still has. Use your knowledge and your own observations to develop your position, and evidence, including the speaker’s own words, to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, supporting evidence, and a conclusion.

title: An Unsung Figure in History
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven essay about a historical figure you think deserves more attention than they get. Choose someone whose story you find compelling, and argue for why they matter.

Make the case for their importance: what they did, what it changed, and why history has under-remembered them. Use your existing knowledge of history and your own observations to develop your position, and evidence to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, supporting evidence, and a conclusion.

title: A Law Worth Debating
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven essay about a law or policy you think should change. Choose one you actually care about — local, national, or global — and argue for what’s wrong with it and what should replace it.

Be fair to the other side: explain why the law exists before you take it apart. Then make your case. Use your knowledge and your own observations to develop your position, and evidence to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, supporting evidence, and a conclusion.

title: A Number That Tells a Story
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven essay about a number, statistic, or trend that tells an important story. Choose data you find striking — about your school, your community, or the world — and argue for what it really shows.

Be careful and honest with the number: explain where it comes from, what it does and doesn’t prove, and why it matters. Make an argument, not just a report. Use the data and your own observations to develop and support your position.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, supporting evidence, and a conclusion.

title: An Experiment Worth Knowing
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven essay about a scientific experiment or study that you think everyone should know about. Choose one that genuinely interests you, and argue for why it matters.

Explain what the experiment asked, what it found, and how it was done — then make a claim about why the result is important or how it changed the way we think. Use your knowledge and your own observations to develop your position, and evidence to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, supporting evidence, and a conclusion.

title: A Place and Its History
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven essay about a place and the history it carries. Choose somewhere real — a neighborhood, a city, a landmark, a region — and argue for what its history reveals about the people who live there or the country it belongs to.

Connect the place to the events, choices, or forces that shaped it. Make a claim about what the place teaches us. Use your knowledge and your own observations to develop your position, and evidence to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, supporting evidence, and a conclusion.

title: A Technology That’s Changing Us
prompt:
Write an essay about a technology that is changing the way we live. Choose one you have real experience with — social media, artificial intelligence, phones, games, or anything else — and argue about whether the change is for better or worse.

Be specific about what the technology does to how we think, connect, or spend our time. Avoid easy answers; make a case you could defend to someone who disagrees. Use your personal experience and observations to develop your position, and evidence from your own life to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: What Success Really Means
prompt:
Write an essay about what success really means. The world offers plenty of definitions — money, fame, grades, happiness — but what do you actually believe, and why?

Develop your own definition and defend it. You might argue against a definition you were handed, or explain how your own has changed. Use your personal experience and observations to develop your position, and evidence from your own life to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: A Tradition Worth Keeping — or Letting Go
prompt:
Write an essay about a tradition and whether it’s worth keeping. Choose a tradition from your family, your culture, your school, or your community, and argue for holding onto it, changing it, or letting it go.

Be honest about what the tradition gives people and what it costs them. Make a case, not just a description. Use your personal experience and observations to develop your position, and evidence from your own life to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.
